contributions.headingText: Elastofibroma is a benign, poorly defined proliferation of fibroelastic tissue with excessive abnormal elastic fibres.
FB51.Y & XH3BQ8 Other specified fibroblastic disorders & Elastofibroma

Elastofibroma most often arises in the deep soft tissue between the lower scapula and the thoracic wall. It may rarely occur in extrascapular locations, including other parts of the thoracic wall, extremities, limb girdles, neck, eyes, oral cavity, and gastrointestinal tract or other viscera. Although elastofibroma is usually a unilateral and solitary mass, bilateral or multiple lesions have been reported.

The lesion usually presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic mass or rarely causes pain, stiffness, scapular snapping, and impingement. CT and MRI show a poorly defined, heterogeneous soft tissue mass with tissue attenuation similar to that of skeletal muscle interlaced with fat strands {8751681}. The lesion may be hypermetabolic on 18F-FDG PET/CT {20978756}.

Although elastofibroma was previously considered to be rare, its exact prevalence is unknown. There is a striking female predominance {7116305}. Elastofibroma occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, with a peak incidence between the seventh and eighth decades of life. The lesions are detectable in 2% of adults aged > 60 years by CT and in 16% of autopsy cases from adults aged > 55 years {9762978; 1124654}.

Subscapular elastofibroma is assumed to be caused by friction of the lower scapula against the thoracic wall due to repetitive minor trauma and manual labour {33952447}. Genetic predisposition of the lesion has also been suggested {7116305}.

Elastotic degeneration of collagen or abnormal elastotic fibrogenesis may underlie the pathogenesis of elastofibroma {13916810; 1842374; 3552953}, and active neovascularization or endothelial–mesenchymal transition plays a potential pathogenetic role {19132384; 25820560}. Elastofibroma often exhibits chromosomal instability including gains of 6p25-q25 and Xq12-q22 and losses of 1p, 13q, 19p, and 22q {12165800; 20422214}. Deletions of CASR (3q13.33-q21.1), GSTP1 (11q13.2), and BRCA2 (13q13.1), as well as gains of APC (5q22.2) and PAH (12q23.2), have also been described {20422214}. Matricellular proteins such as periostin and tenascin-C may be involved in its pathogenesis {25820560}.
The lesion is poorly defined and rubbery, composed of grey or whitish fibrous tissue with variable intervening streaks of yellow fatty tissue. The diameter ranges from 20 to 150 mm.

Elastofibroma is composed predominantly of fibrocollagenous tissue containing a large number of abnormal elastic fibres and dispersed, bland-appearing spindle cells, admixed with a variable amount of adipose tissue and small blood vessels. A focally myxoid matrix is common. The elastic fibres are typically thick or coarse, deeply eosinophilic, and fragmented into linearly arranged globular or serrated disc-like structures, simulating beads on a string, which are highlighted using elastic stains. Immunohistochemically, the spindle cells are positive for CD34, but negative for SMA, desmin, and S100 {16133360; 25820560}.
Cytology aspirate shows fibrocollagenous tissue fragments and spindle cells, with scattered linear (braid-like), globular, or stellate structures of degenerate elastic fibres (Pap) {14648789}.
Essential: a bland, hypocellular fibrofatty tumour with excessive abnormal elastic fibres.
Elastofibroma is a benign lesion and is cured by simple excision. Local recurrence is exceptional.
